questions.evidenceQuote: In the late 1940s, social psychologists Leon Festinger, Stan Schachter, and Kurt Back were also interested in distance and relationships when they set out to examine friendship formation in two MIT residential complexes: Westgate and Westgate West. Unlike the city of Philadelphia, there were no ethnic enclaves—no Chinatown where Chinese immigrants would gravitate, for example—so the selection effect (i.e., a resident choosing to live in a particular area) was kept to a minimum.

questions.evidenceQuote: Festinger and colleagues knew exactly where all the participants in this study lived, and asked one simple question: “What three people in Westgate or Westgate West do you see most of socially?” In the microcosm of a college dorm, their research replicated the Philadelphia and Dutch findings: 112 out of the possible 187 friendship nominations, or 60 percent, lived next door or in the unit connected directly through staircases. Only seven nominations were made of someone living four units away or more. So, physical distance clearly matters.

questions.evidenceQuote: The other interesting finding from the study was that functional distance also matters. Those who lived close to the staircases were far more likely to become friends with someone living on a different floor than those who lived farther away from the staircases. What this suggests is that physical and functional distance dictate the probability of a chance meeting, and that the more frequently one meets someone informally, the more likely it is that a friendship emerges.

questions.evidenceQuote: At their best, social psychologists work by identifying an association between two variables in the real world (e.g., residential proximity and friendship), then test causal mechanisms, or what accounts for the observed correlation. What repeated chance meetings do is increase familiarity. Bob Zajonc, one of the greatest social psychologists of all time, zeroed in on the familiarity effect, or what he called the “mere exposure effect,” in a series of experiments.

questions.evidenceQuote: Even before he conducted this series of experiments, Zajonc made an ingenious refinement of previous research on word frequency and its link to perceived “desirability” of a word (i.e., how good or bad a word sounds). Word frequency was measured by how often each word appeared in published books and magazines in the 1920s and 1930s, in painstaking work conducted by Edward Thorndike and Irving Lorge. Desirability was determined by aggregating English speakers’ ratings of various English words.

specificFindings: Festinger,Schachter and Back examine friendship formation in MIT Westgate/WestgateWest in the late1940s,not the preceding marriage study or all undergraduate grades. No unstated resident identities are added.
The nomination question asks three people seen most socially. It is not three closest romantic partners,largest rooms or marriage histories. Addresses are known separately for distance analysis.

Seven counts nominations at four-or-more units,not total residents,seven percent or staircases. The surrounding112of187/about60percent finding has a different category and unit from Philadelphia marriage licences.

Physical distance matters is the authors conclusion from the nomination pattern,not proof of a sole sufficient cause of every friendship. Functional distance adds actual circulation routes and cross-floor meeting opportunities.

Repeated chance meetings are linked to familiarity,not objectively identical personal traits or guaranteed friendship. Zero in on means focus; the familiarity/mere-exposure names are preserved without treating the greatest-psychologist phrase as a new objective ranking.
Refinement of prior word-frequency/desirability work precedes the described series of experiments. No invented precise year or reversal to after the classroom field experiment is added.

Thorndike and Lorge count book/magazine occurrences from1920s/1930s. English-speaker desirability ratings are a different measure and source from word frequency; neither is a pronunciation-time count.

The good/better opening plays on ordinary comparative meaning before frequency and liking scores. Better remains the comparative word; good being liked more does not redefine English grammar or prove a literal census of all speakers.

If/then/should gives a conditional prediction. Indeed introduces reported good-over-better desirability ratings consistent with it. The original references participants in an experiment,but the natural word-frequency comparison still remains correlational as the next paragraph explicitly states; experimental collection of ratings alone does not manipulate prior natural frequency.

Still correlational and cannot infer causal effect limit the earlier result. They do not prove no causal effect can exist or erase the observations,which motivates the new unfamiliar-stimulus experiment.

Iktitaf,afworbu,saricik are nonsense stimuli,not genuine Turkish vocabulary to teach. The experimenters Turkish label and the authors they-werent parenthesis are distinguished rather than endorsing the cover description as fact.

Pronunciation follows demonstration and precedes guessing good/bad meaning. The task is an affective guess,not accurate dictionary translation or recalling magazine occurrence counts; relevant distractors were refined before review.

Familiarity is manipulated through once/twice versus ten/twenty-five presentations,not by changing nationalities,positive definitions or claiming every count identical. Manipulate is experimental variable control,not a website instruction to deceive users.

The next replication uses Chinese characters and the subsequent one uses graduation photos. A stimulus script does not imply all participants are native readers or that every possible material must yield identical effects.
Doesnt stop here introduces extension to Moreland/Zajonc field experiment in a real college classroom. It is not retracting the lab findings or calling them fictional.

The casually dressed actors are the women research assistants following entry/staircase/seating instructions. Casual style does not assert identical outfits,all students dressed the same or lack of care in the experiment.

More exposure associated with perceived similarity is distinguished from verified objective personality,genes or biographies. The book later attributes a perceived-similarity-to-attraction relationship to previous research; that is not an inevitable marriage outcome.
Nobody said yes to knowing the women differs from very few saying they had seen them. Neither is proof nobody was exposed; explicit personal recognition and familiarity ratings are distinct measures.

Final question quotes only its target prior-research sentence,leaving other unassigned mechanism conclusions pending. All25 authored targets add exactly25 direct IDs and all published fingerprints are unchanged.
